t: Previous Permutation With One Swap — Greedy on the First Descent
o:
We must produce the lexicographically largest array strictly smaller than `arr` using **exactly one swap** (swapping equal values counts as a swap but changes nothing, so it can't help make a smaller array). To get *any* smaller array we need a position $i$ where `arr[i] > arr[j]` for some later $j$; to keep the result as large as possible we should change the array as far right as possible and by as little as possible.

**Example 1:** `[3,2,1]` — the only descent is at index 0 (`3 > 2`). The largest value after index 0 that is smaller than 3 is 2; among duplicates of 2 we take the leftmost occurrence (index 1). Swapping gives `[3,1,2]`.

**Example 2:** `[1,1,5]` is non-decreasing, so no swap can make it smaller — return it unchanged.

**Example 3:** `[1,9,4,6,7]` — scan from the right: `7 > 6 > 4`, so index 1 (`9`) is the first element greater than its successor. The largest value smaller than 9 in the suffix is 7 (index 4). Swap → `[1,7,4,6,9]`.

With $n \le 10^4$ even an $O(n^2)$ scan fits easily, but a single backward pass achieves $O(n)$.
k: A swap makes the array smaller iff it involves some index i with arr[i] > arr[j] for j > i; if arr is non-decreasing no valid swap exists.
To maximize the result, pick the RIGHTMOST such i (the first descent scanning from the back) — changing earlier positions loses more lexicographic value.
Swap arr[i] with the LARGEST value in the suffix that is strictly less than arr[i]; among ties take the LEFTMOST occurrence to keep the tail as large as possible.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Swaps
a.i: Try every pair $(i, j)$ with $i < j$, perform the swap, and keep the best (largest) result that is strictly smaller than the original. With $n \le 10^4$ this is up to ~$5\times10^7$ pair checks per comparison-heavy copy, which is borderline but acceptable for the given constraints. It directly mirrors the problem definition and needs no insight.
s: Copy arr as the original; initialize answer = arr.
For each pair i < j, swap arr[i], arr[j]; if the result is strictly smaller than the original and larger than the current answer, record it.
Return the recorded answer (or the original array if none improved).
a.t: O(n^2) pairs, each with an O(n) comparison/copy — O(n^3) worst case, ~10^12 ops at n=10^4, too slow in practice despite fitting constraints loosely; fine conceptually.
a.sp: O(n) for the stored best answer.

a.i: Scan from the right to find the first index $i$ where `arr[i] > arr[i+1]`. Any swap not involving such a 'descent' position cannot shrink the array, and swapping at the *rightmost* descent keeps the changed prefix minimal, hence the result maximal. Then find the largest value in `arr[i+1..]` that is strictly less than `arr[i]`; if several positions hold that value, use the leftmost one so the untouched tail stays as large as possible. One swap finishes the job.
s: Iterate i from n-2 down to 0; stop at the first i with arr[i] > arr[i+1]. If none exists, return arr unchanged.
Find j = i+1 initially; extend j while j+1 < n and arr[j+1] < arr[i] and arr[j+1] >= arr[j], moving j to the leftmost occurrence of the maximum value below arr[i].
a.t: O(n) — two linear scans over the array.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — the swap is done in place.

w: In an interview, go straight to the greedy two-pass solution: state the three facts (need a descent, prefer the rightmost descent, prefer the largest-but-smaller value with leftmost tie-break), then code it — it's ~10 lines. Common pitfalls: (1) using `>=` instead of `>` when searching for the descent breaks on non-strictly-increasing tails like `[1,1,5]`; (2) picking the *rightmost* duplicate when tie-breaking — e.g. `[3,1,1,3]` must become `[1,3,1,3]` via swapping index 0 with the first 1, not the last; (3) forgetting that a non-decreasing array has no answer. Edge cases: length 1, all-equal elements, already-sorted input. Follow-ups: generalize to k swaps (related to 'previous permutation' via `std::prev_permutation`-style algorithm), or handle streams/large n where O(n) matters.
